--- title: "Prediction and explanation" description: "A fitted model can be used to predict new cases or to explain what drives the outcome. A variable can help the first and mislead the second, and the model's output gives no warning." order: 3 categories: [foundations, interpretation] --- ## Two uses for one model [The previous page](what-is-machine-learning.qmd) contrasted two aims: estimating an effect and predicting new cases. The same fitted model can serve either aim, but the two are checked in very different ways. - **Prediction** estimates the outcome for cases the model has not seen. It is checked directly: hold some cases back from fitting, predict them, and measure the error. An input that lowers that error is useful, whatever the reason it helps. - **Explanation** claims a cause: if an input changed, with everything else held fixed, the outcome would change. The data alone cannot check that. It needs an experiment or knowledge of the system. ::: {.diagram} ![Prediction and explanation compared. Explanation asks more of the model and is harder to check.](img/prediction-and-explanation.svg){fig-alt="At the top, one box reads 'One model fitted to the data', with arrows to two columns. Prediction, in orange: a curve through scattered points with a new case marked on it; the question is the outcome for a case the model has not seen, the answer is a value for each new case, and it is checked by the error on cases held back from fitting. Explanation, in green: depth points to both salinity and the outcome, and a crossed-out dashed line joins salinity to the outcome; the question is whether changing an input changes the outcome, the answer is a claim about cause and effect, and it is checked by study design and knowledge of the system, not by the data alone. A bar along the bottom runs from orange to green: explanation asks more of the model and is harder to check."} ::: A variable can do well for one aim and badly for the other. The example below shows salinity doing exactly that. ## Depth confounds the salinity slope ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the data on this page The coastal survey used here is **simulated**, not a real survey. That is deliberate: because we wrote the generating process (`R/make-example-data.R`), we know the true relationships and can show whether a model recovers them. No real survey is being misrepresented, and the figures are not results about any real species. See `data/README.md` for what is built into it. ::: A **confounder** is a variable that affects both an input and the outcome, so the two move together even when neither affects the other. In this simulated survey salinity has no effect on the species. It rises with depth, though, and depth does matter: the species is most common around 80 m. Depth is the confounder. Three models are fitted to the same training stations. Each bends the temperature line with a squared term, as the previous page suggested trying. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} survey <- load_coastal_survey() split <- initial_split(survey, prop = 0.75) train <- training(split) test <- testing(split) formulas <- list( "Temperature" = abundance ~ temperature_c + I(temperature_c^2), "Temperature + salinity" = abundance ~ temperature_c + I(temperature_c^2) + salinity_psu, "Temperature + salinity + depth" = abundance ~ temperature_c + I(temperature_c^2) + salinity_psu + depth_m + I(depth_m^2) ) fits <- map(formulas, \(f) fit(linear_reg(), f, data = train)) ``` ::: ### For prediction, salinity can stand in for depth The test stations were held back from fitting, so the error on them shows how well each model predicts new stations: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} imap(fits, \(fit, name) { augment(fit, test) |> rmse(abundance, .pred) |> transmute(model = name, test_rmse = round(.estimate, 2)) }) |> list_rbind() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|model | test_rmse| |:------------------------------|---------:| |Temperature | 4.38| |Temperature + salinity | 4.33| |Temperature + salinity + depth | 4.25|
::: ::: Adding salinity lowers the error slightly, because it carries a little of depth's information. For prediction that is allowed: nothing more is asked of an input than that it helps. ### For explanation, the salinity slope misleads In the second model the salinity slope is about −2.2: each extra unit of salinity goes with about 2.2 fewer animals. Its 95% interval stays well clear of zero, the value that would mean no relationship (@fig-salinity). Read as a cause, that slope says freshening the water would bring more animals. It would not. Once depth enters the model, the salinity slope shrinks to about −0.2 and its interval includes zero. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} slopes <- imap(fits[-1], \(fit, name) { tidy(fit, conf.int = TRUE) |> filter(term == "salinity_psu") |> mutate(model = name) }) |> list_rbind() ggplot(slopes, aes(estimate, model)) + geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = ml_palette[["grey"]]) + geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = conf.low, xmax = conf.high), height = 0.15, colour = ml_palette[["blue"]], linewidth = 1) + geom_point(size = 3, colour = ml_palette[["blue"]]) + labs(x = "Salinity slope (animals per unit of salinity)", y = NULL) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![The salinity slope, with its 95% interval, in the two models that include salinity. Without depth, salinity appears to matter. With depth, its slope shrinks to near zero, which is the true value built into the simulation.](prediction-and-explanation_files/figure-html/fig-salinity-1.png){#fig-salinity fig-alt='Two horizontal interval bars on an axis of salinity slope. For the model without depth, the estimate is about minus 2.2 with an interval from about minus 3.3 to minus 1.2, clear of the dashed zero line. For the model with depth, the estimate is about minus 0.2 with an interval from about minus 1.6 to 1.2, spanning zero.' width=1400} ::: ::: A confounder can be dealt with only by measuring it, as here, by knowing from the system that it is there, or by an experiment that changes the input alone. Had depth not been recorded, the second model would have a lower test error than the first and a confident salinity slope, and nothing in its output would point to depth. Test error cannot reveal a confounder. That is why explanation needs study design and knowledge of the system. ## Key points ::: {.key-points} - Prediction estimates the outcome for new cases and is checked on held-back data. - Explanation claims a cause, and rests on study design and knowledge of the system, not on the data alone. - A confounder affects both an input and the outcome. It can give the input a confident slope while the input causes nothing, as depth does for salinity here. - Test error cannot reveal a confounder. Measuring it or knowing about it can. - Decide which aim you have before choosing a model and its variables. ::: ## Try it yourself Drop `salinity_psu` from the third model. Does the test error change, and do the depth terms move? Then fit `abundance ~ salinity_psu` alone and compare its slope with the one in @fig-salinity.
